question: Young people’s independence, or the process of young people’s transition from dependence on their parents to independent living, is one of the key stages in life. According to data from 2022, 49.4 % of young people (aged 18-34) in the European Union live with at least one of their parents. More than a third of these young people are in stable employment. 1.

How does the Commission promote the empowerment of young people through its policies, programmes and initiatives, and are there any long-term Commission strategies addressing this issue? Financial literacy is crucial in the process of youth empowerment, as it provides young people with independence and security in life. In September 2007, the Commission, together with the OECD, adopted a financial competence framework for children and youth in the EU.

Could the Commission submit a report every six months on the impact of the financial competence framework for children and youth in the EU, so that we might gain an insight into its usefulness and visibility?
answer: The 2021 Council Resolution (1) promotes the empowerment of young people through the development of eight key competences for lifelong learning (2) from early childhood education and care to adult learning and combines formal, nonformal and informal learning.

Based on the 2018 Council Recommendation (3), the Commission has established more detailed competence frameworks for entrepreneurial competence (EntreComp), digital competence (DigiComp), personal, social, and learning to learn competence (LifeComp), and education for sustainability (GreenComp). Key competences for lifelong learning are also promoted through the Erasmus+ programme.

The Commission considers that financial literacy and empowerment are closely linked. As part of the Commission policies to improve financial literacy, several measures, including the publication of the financial competence framework for children and youth in the EU in September 2023 (4), will contribute to increasing financial literacy.

In order to measure levels of financial literacy across the Member States a Eurobarometer survey (5) was carried out in 2023. As the financial competence framework is voluntary, its uptake by Member States and stakeholders will not be uniform. In addition, as it was only recently published, we do not have detailed information on its impact to date.

The Commission, however, will remain in close contact with Member States on the uptake of the framework and will use future Eurobarometer surveys to periodically measure levels of financial literacy in the EU. A six-month reporting period would be too short to identify clear results on the impact of the framework.

Council Resolution on a strategic framework for European cooperation in education and training towards the European Education Area and beyond (20212030) , OJ C 66, 26.2.2021, p. 1-21; https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?
